newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief departs for neighbouring states.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief departs for neighbouring states.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila left his headquarters in southeast Zaire on Thursday to visit neighbouring countries before a first face-to-face meeting with President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Officials said Kabila would travel to some next-door countries, which they did not name, before flying to South Africa and then on to the talks, now rescheduled for Saturday.
Zaire's information minister told Reuters on Thursday the Mobutu-Kabila meeting, originally set for Friday aboard a South African naval ship, had been postponed till Saturday.
Rebel officials in Lubumbashi were unaware of the change and said South African President Nelson Mandela, brokering the peace initiative as an African solution, would contact Kabila direct.

The rebel chief, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, told Reuters late Wednesday his meeting with Mobutu would discuss the Zairean president's departure from power after 32 years.
"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," Kabila said.
As the talks were finalised, Kabila's forces advanced towards the town of Kenge on the way to Kinshasa.
Kabila said Mobutu's army had begun blowing up bridges to try to slow the military push.
"They have started blowing up bridges in Kenge in order to stop our forces from advancing to Kinshasa. But that will not hinder us and if necessary we shall swim," Kabila said.
A mining expert who arrived in Lubumbashi from the area on Thursday told Reuters the rebels were advancing from the towns of Ilebo, Tshikapa, Kananga and Kikwit.

The expert, who declined to be named, said rebels from Ilebo and Kananga were advancing on foot while those from Tshikapa and Kikwit were using tanks and armoured personnel carriers and had long-range artillery pieces and bridge laying equipment.

"It's big stuff. These guys are heavily equipped and should have no problems crossing the rivers in that area to Kenge and Kinshasa because they are equipped with bridge-laying gear and speed boats," he added.
The rebels have said would will enter Kinshasa within the next 10 to 15 days. The expert agreed with that: "From what I saw, that timescale makes a lot of sense. These guys are serious."
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson told reporters in Kinshasa on Wednesday there were no preconditions for the talks, due to be chaired by Mandela.

But in Lubumbashi, Kabila said he had not softened his position that Mobutu must agree to stand down. The rebel leader's aides said he had been surprised by Richardson's announcement in Kinshasa that "several African leaders" would attend the talks on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua.
The rebels do not want the talks to turn into a mini-summit about one of Africa's biggest political shake-ups for decades.
There was no indication Mobutu had agreed to step down.
In talks with Kabila on Tuesday, Richardson did not persuade him to accept a ceasefire ahead of the meeting or make agree to accept a transitional government before elections.
"There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," Kabila said.
He launched his rebellion in Zaire last October and rebels have made short shrift of Mobutu's ragged army and are poised to attack Kinshasa from Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) to the east.
